newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asia markets mixed after second Iraq attack.
newsitem.headline: Asia markets mixed after second Iraq attack.

text.p: Oil prices firmed briefly in Asia after the U.S. launched another attack against Iraq, but other markets had a more muted response to the news which traders saw as a mopping up exercise rather than a new assault.
Crude oil futures jumped $0.30 a barrel to $23.65 a barrel after news that the U.S. Navy fired 17 Tomahawk missiles at air defence targets in southern Iraq.
The action came a day after the United States launched 27 of the precision weapons at similar targets in the area.
Oil prices later eased to $23.37 as the market awaited further news from Washington and the United Nations.

Iraq had been expected to resume oil sales this month for the first time since its 1990 invasion of Kuwait but the United Nations delayed the plan after Iraqi troops moved against Kurds in northern regions. "The (oil) market is nervous and cautious. Reaction to the second missile attack seems to be relatively calm after a similar situation yesterday," an oil trader in Tokyo said.
In foreign exchange trading the dollar held steady against most currencies and was quoted at 109.28/31 against 109.24/31 at the close in New York on Tuesday.
"We don't see the typical 'dollar-buying in a crisis' because it isn't a crisis," said Koji Asano, senior manager at Fuji Bank.
Gold prices in Hong Kong and Tokyo showed little reaction to the latest attack. The metal was quoted at US$386.30/386.80 in Tokyo at midmorning versus $386.15/386/55 in New York on Tuesday.
Regional equities markets had mixed reactions.
In Tokyo, the market recovered initial weakness which came amid surprise over the second round of attacks. Traders had considered Tuesday's assault a one-time event.
The key Nikkei 225-share index fell 16.38 points to 20,066.02 on the news but clawed its way back by mid-afternoon to 20,201.87, up 3.72 points or 0.02 percent from Monday.

"Wall Street as well as Tokyo thought the fiasco was over and just part of President Clinton's election campaign. Anxiety was fading when the second round came," said Keiji Arai, strategist at Sanyo Securities.

In Taiwan, stocks ended lower amid concern over the rising tensions in the Gulf, with the weighted index down 29.19 points or 0.47 percent, at 6,228.78. Thai stocks were lower but the market had stabilised after initial jitters over the conflict.
A firmer ending on Wall Street helped sentiment when trading resumed in Asia, some traders said.
After steep early falls, U.S. stocks recovered when a fresh batch of economic data did not prove as strong as feared.
The news dashed fears the Federal Reserve would push interest rates higher.

But while the news was encouraging, traders noted that most of the 32 point gain in the Dow Jones Industrial Average reflected a rise in the price of energy company stocks, which are benefiting from the higher oil prices.
Still, the rise in the Dow gave Indonesia shares a boost at the opening.

"The rise in the Dow overnight coupled with generally stronger regional markets has improved market sentiment, but the volume remains slim and many brokers are on the sidelines," one trader in Jakarta said.
Hong Kong stocks rebounded on a belief a selloff on Tuesday was overdone. The Hang Seng Index was up 103.73 points, or 0.95 percent, at 11,060.91.
